Well, no, I wouldn't say that. I still like the things I've always liked, honestly. It’s not like that. 

Like, for instance, I have this thing I do on the weekends. So I’ll toss them in the trunk of my car and take them home to work on. And I still really, really enjoy doing that. I’ll be out in the garage for hours with the WD-40 and a pad of steel wool, just scrubbing the rust off the spokes, getting black grease all over my hands and under my fingernails. My wife always gets on my case about tracking the grease into the kitchen, but... anyway, when I’m out there, I still get that same exact good feeling when I finally get a rusted-out chain moving smoothly again, or when I get the brakes calibrated just right. 

Or, you know, if I’m watching a baseball game on a Sunday afternoon, and my team actually manages to pull off a win in the bottom of the ninth inning, I’m still jumping up off the couch cheering. I still get really into it. So the things I like... I still like them just as much as I ever did. It’s not that my hobbies have stopped being fun or anything like that. Yeah, well, like I was kind of rambling about a few minutes ago, it really is bleeding into absolutely everything I do. I mean, like I said, I still get the actual physical cleaning done at work—the buffing, the mopping, the trash—but because I'm so much slower now, and because I'm constantly second-guessing my logs and my supply counts, it just drains everything out of me. Usually, I'm the guy with the clipboard, right? I've got a mental list of who is bringing the heavy-duty trash bags, who has the wheelbarrows, whose truck we're using to haul all the brush and junk to the dump. But because my memory is just acting like a sieve right now, I couldn't even fathom trying to keep all those moving parts straight in my head. I'd probably tell three different people to bring rakes and completely forget to ask anyone to bring work gloves, or I'd forget what time I told everyone to meet at the creek. It's just... it's embarrassing to even think about messing it up. So I just skipped the whole thing this year. Didn't even participate. 

And it's the exact same story with the family get-togethers. I brought up my niece's birthday party earlier—she just turned seven, big dinosaur-themed party my sister-in-law threw in their backyard—and I just couldn't do it. When you're at those things, people are talking to you, telling you about their new jobs or their kids' schools or whatever, and you have to actually pay attention and remember what they're saying to hold a normal conversation. And I just know I'd be standing there by the snack table, completely zoning out, not absorbing a single word my own brother is saying to me, and then I'd look like a jerk for not listening. So I just stay home. I used to always make time for that stuff, you know? I was always the guy organizing things, showing up early to help set up the folding chairs and the coolers. Now I'm just skipping it all because I can't trust my own head to keep up with even a basic conversation, let alone coordinate anything.

Oh, yeah. Sleep... sleep is a whole other ordeal. It's been messed up for a really long time now, honestly. I don't even remember the last time I woke up feeling actually good.

It's like I was just lying there with my eyes closed but my body didn't actually do any recharging. I'll hear my alarm go off, just that awful standard beeping sound on my phone, and I feel like I've been hit by a truck. My body feels like lead. Well, no... I wouldn't say *problems*, exactly. I mean, not in the sense of arguments or people being mad at me, if that's what you mean. 

Take my wife, for example. Like I mentioned earlier with the blackout curtains and the lawn, she is just an absolute saint about all this. And as for my family or my friends... it's kind of the same deal. Like my brother, the one whose kid had the dinosaur party I was telling you about that I skipped. I called him that morning and just told him I was completely wiped out from work. And since they all know I work those graveyard shifts, hauling trash and running floor machines all night, they just kind of accept it. They just think, "Oh, he's just exhausted from the schedule, let him sleep." They don't really push back or lay on a guilt trip. 

Same with the guys in the neighborhood. When I bailed on the spring clean-up, my buddy Mark—he lives two doors down, the guy who usually brings the wheelbarrows—he just texted me back and said, "No worries man, get some rest, we'll catch you next time." So nobody is yelling at me or cutting me off or anything. I guess I'm the one pulling away and isolating myself, but they aren't holding it against me. They just think I'm busy or worn out from the job. Honestly, sometimes I almost wish they *would* get a little mad, just so I'd feel like I wasn't just fading into the background, you know? But no, to answer your question, no actual problems or arguments with anyone. Everyone's been really understanding.

Motivation... yeah, um, that is really the crux of the whole issue right there. It is incredibly hard to get motivated, even on my days off. Especially on my days off, honestly. Because, like I was saying before, my schedule is already so completely backwards from working the graveyard shift at the office building, so my body is always a little confused anyway. And then the coffee gets cold, and I'm just sitting there staring at the mug, and the whole sequence of events—putting on my work boots, walking out to the shed, checking the gas in the mower, pulling the cord—it all just piles up in my head until it feels like someone is asking me to climb Mount Everest.

It really goes right back to what I was trying to explain earlier about the Camry, and even the neighborhood clean-up with Mark. The desire to have a nice lawn or a working car is completely intact. And the worst part is, it's so incredibly frustrating because I will literally spend three or four hours sitting in that chair, feeling absolutely awful and guilty about not doing the chore, when the chore itself would have only taken me half an hour. I spend more energy beating myself up over not starting than I would have spent just doing it. 

It's like my starter motor is completely busted, even if the engine itself is fine once I finally get it running. So yeah, the motivation to initiate things is just... it's practically zero right now.
